content: Testing with same-day results using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) in antenatal care is particularly useful for pregnant women who present late in pregnancy, arrive only during labor, or have not received their HIV results prior to labor. The procedure should be explained to the patient, and consent must be obtained in accordance with national policy. Only test kits recommended by national or international bodies should be used, and the manufacturer's instructions for the selected HIV rapid test must be followed. Before testing, prepare a worksheet, label the test, and record the batch number and expiry date, ensuring the test has not expired. Wear gloves when drawing blood and adhere to standard safety precautions for waste disposal. Inform the patient about the expected wait time for results, whether same-day or requiring a return visit. Blood for all required tests, such as hemoglobin (Hb), syphilis, and HIV, should be drawn at the same time. Use a sterile needle and syringe for venous blood collection or a lancet for a finger prick. Perform the test according to the manufacturer's instructions and interpret the results as specified. If the first HIV test result is negative, no further testing is needed, and the result should be recorded as HIV-negative. If the first test result is positive, a second HIV rapid test using a different test kit must be performed. If the second test is also positive, record the result as HIV-positive. If the first test is positive but the second is negative, repeat the testing using a finger prick and both test kits. If both repeat tests are positive or negative, record the result accordingly. If the results differ, use another test or record the results as inconclusive. Inconclusive results require retesting after two weeks or referral to a hospital for confirmatory testing. All results should be sent to the health worker, and patient confidentiality must be respected. For umbilical cord care, 1% chlorhexidine digluconate (delivering 4% chlorhexidine) in gel or liquid form should be used. Additional supplies for antenatal and childbirth care include proteinuria dipsticks, urine collection containers, HIV testing kits (two types), and hemoglobin testing kits. Urine protein testing involves labeling a clean container, instructing the patient on how to collect a clean-catch urine sample, and analyzing the sample using either a dipstick or boiling method. For the dipstick method, dip the coated end into the urine, shake off excess, wait the specified time, and compare the color to the chart on the label. For the boiling method, boil the top half of the urine in a test tube, allow it to stand, and add 2-3 drops of 2-3% acetic acid. Cloudiness after boiling indicates protein presence, while clearing after adding acetic acid suggests no protein. Hemoglobin testing requires drawing blood with a sterile needle and syringe or lancet, following local instructions. Malaria testing can be done using light microscopy or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), depending on local resources and needs. For syphilis testing using the rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test, obtain consent, explain the procedure, and draw 5 mL of venous blood into a test tube. Allow the serum to separate by sitting for 20 minutes or centrifuging for 3-5 minutes. Use a pipette to withdraw serum without including red blood cells, and place one drop (50 µL) on a test card circle. Spread the serum evenly, add one drop (20 µL) of antigen, and rotate the card for 8 minutes. Inspect for clumping under good light: No clumping indicates a non-reactive (negative) result. Visible clumping indicates a reactive (positive) result. Minimal clumping suggests a weakly reactive (positive) result. Pregnant women should visit a health center as early as possible and at least four times during pregnancy, even if no problems arise. Health workers will monitor health, provide treatments, and offer counseling on breastfeeding, birth spacing, nutrition, HIV testing, and other health matters. Women should bring their maternal health record to every visit. During pregnancy, women should eat a healthy diet, take prescribed supplements, rest, avoid heavy lifting, sleep under an insecticide-treated bed net, and avoid alcohol, smoking, and unprescribed medications. Condom use is recommended to prevent sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or HIV if at risk. Signs of labor include painful contractions every 20 minutes or less, rupture of membranes, and bloody discharge. Danger signs requiring immediate medical attention include vaginal bleeding, convulsions, severe headaches with blurred vision, fever with weakness, severe abdominal pain, and difficulty breathing. After birth, mothers should eat nutritious foods, take iron tablets, rest, drink clean water, and avoid alcohol, smoking, and unprescribed medications. They should practice good hygiene, including washing the perineum daily and changing pads every 4-6 hours. Family planning is essential, as pregnancy can occur within weeks after delivery if not exclusively breastfeeding. Newborn care includes keeping the baby clean, warm, and dry, and ensuring proper umbilical cord care. Breastfeeding should begin within one hour of birth and continue exclusively for six months. Breast milk provides all necessary nutrients and protects against infections. Mothers should drink plenty of water and seek help from health workers if breastfeeding difficulties arise. Routine postnatal visits should occur within 24 hours, on day 3, between days 7-14, and at six weeks postpartum. Danger signs in newborns requiring immediate care include difficulty breathing, fever, fits, feeding problems, diarrhea, or signs of infection.
